Automation alone does not determine the future society, because the decisive question is who owns the automated productive systems, data, energy and land, and who therefore receives their output and income. In the first scenario, automation raises physical productive capacity while access to food, housing, health care and other necessities remains conditional on wages or private wealth. As paid human work disappears, most people lose both purchasing power and their normal route to the goods that machines can abundantly produce, so a society can have full warehouses and widespread deprivation at the same time. Owners of robots, platforms, patents, energy systems and scarce land would capture much of the income, creating a small capital-owning class alongside a permanently unemployed or precariously employed majority. The market would then become unstable because automated firms can make goods cheaply but cannot profitably sell them to a population without income, encouraging debt, cut-price provision, monopolies and government emergency support rather than a healthy mass-consumer economy. Population growth would sharpen competition for whatever remains genuinely scarce, especially desirable locations, natural resources, personal attention, political influence and exclusive experiences, even if routine manufactured goods are cheap. Mass joblessness would also be a social crisis rather than merely an income crisis, because employment commonly supplies time structure, relationships, collective activity, status, purpose and identity, and job loss is associated with worsening mental health. A likely political outcome is recurring conflict over ownership and distribution, ranging from labour movements and demands for dividends to riots, populist mobilisation or demands to halt automation. The most dangerous version becomes an automated oligarchy, in which concentrated wealth purchases political influence and surveillance systems are used to manage excluded populations rather than to empower them. Such a regime could be technically efficient yet politically brittle, because economic exclusion and unaccountable automated decisions undermine legitimacy. A democratic government trying to prevent that outcome would need to separate survival from employment through measures such as a guaranteed income or services, broad ownership of automation, taxes or royalties on automated profits, and strong anti-monopoly rules. It would also need public auditability of consequential algorithms, appeal rights against automated decisions, data rights, cybersecurity safeguards and human responsibility for systems that allocate benefits, policing, credit or legal outcomes. Without redistribution, however, this first scenario is not a stable “post-work” society but a society that retains automation while making livelihood dependent on an increasingly unavailable job. In the second scenario, automated production is paired with universal access to the resources required for a dignified life, so food, shelter, health care, education, energy, communications and mobility are guaranteed independently of employment. This could be organised as universal public services, an unconditional basic income, a social dividend from publicly or broadly owned automated capital, or a combination of these arrangements. A universal basic income is a periodic unconditional payment made to individuals regardless of wealth or employment, while a universal-resource system can go further by directly guaranteeing essential services. The economic circuit would work because robots supply much of production, the public captures part of the resulting surplus through ownership, taxes, resource rents or dividends, and people receive purchasing power or direct access with which to claim the output. In this setting, a job becomes voluntary rather than a condition of survival, and people may choose paid work, caregiving, art, study, research, local government, sport, friendship or entrepreneurship according to interest rather than necessity. The society would still need institutions that create recognition and belonging, because an income guarantee does not automatically replace the purpose, accomplishment and identity that many people obtain through work. Schools, civic associations, cooperatives, cultural institutions and voluntary public-service programmes would therefore become more important as places where people develop skill, contribution, status and community without coercive employment. Governance would shift from chiefly regulating labour markets toward democratically deciding what is universal, how automation’s surplus is shared, which scarce goods are rationed or priced, and which technologies are permitted. Universal provision would not mean that every scarce luxury is free, so transparent allocation rules, democratic budgeting and protected basic entitlements would be needed to prevent informal privilege from replacing market inequality. The durable version of this second society is therefore neither rule by machines nor passive leisure for everyone, but democratic control of automated infrastructure combined with guaranteed material security and meaningful voluntary human participation.

CAMBRIDGE, Mass., May 17, 2023 – The Dark Ages were not entirely dark. Advances in agriculture and building technology increased Medieval wealth and led to a wave of cathedral construction in Europe. However, it was a time of profound inequality. Elites captured virtually all economic gains. In Britain, as Canterbury Cathedral soared upward, peasants had no net increase in wealth between 1100 and 1300. Life expectancy hovered around 25 years. Chronic malnutrition was rampant.
“We’ve been struggling to share prosperity for a long time,” says MIT professor “Every cathedral that your parents dragged you to see in Europe is a symbol of despair and expropriation, made possible by higher productivity.”
At a glance, this might not seem relevant to life in 2023. But Johnson and his MIT colleague both economists, think it is. Technology drives economic progress. As innovations take hold, one perpetual question is: Who benefits?
This applies, the scholars believe, to automation and artificial intelligence, which is the focus of a new book by Acemoglu and Johnson, “Power and Progress: Our 1000-Year Struggle Over Technology and Prosperity,” published this week by PublicAffairs. In it, they examine who reaped the rewards from past innovations and who may gain from AI today, economically and politically.
“The book is about the choices we make with technology,” Johnson says. “That’s a very MIT type of theme. But a lot of people feel technology just descends on you, and you have to live with it.”
AI could develop as a beneficial force, Johnson says. However, he adds, “Many algorithms are being designed to try to replace humans as much as possible. We think that’s entirely wrong. The way we make progress with technology is by making machines useful to people, not displacing them. In the past we have had automation, but with new tasks for people to do and sufficient countervailing power in society.”
Today, AI is a tool of social control for some governments that also creates riches for a small number of people, according to Acemoglu and Johnson. “The current path of AI is neither good for the economy nor for democracy, and these two problems, unfortunately, reinforce each other,” they write.
A return to shared prosperity?
Acemoglu and Johnson have collaborated before; in the early 2000s, with political scientist James Robinson, they produced influential papers about politics and economic progress. Acemoglu, an Institute Professor at MIT, also co-authored with Robinson the books “Why Nations Fail” (2012), about political institutions and growth, and “The Narrow Corridor” (2019), which casts liberty as the never-assured outcome of social struggle.
Johnson, the Ronald A. Kurtz Professor of Entrepreneurship at the MIT Sloan School of Management, wrote “13 Bankers” (2010), about finance reform, and, with MIT economist Jonathan Gruber, “Jump-Starting America” (2019), a call for more investment in scientific research.
In “Power and Progress,” the authors emphasize that technology has created remarkable long-term benefits. As they write, “we are greatly better off than our ancestors,” and “scientific and technological progress is a vital part of that story.”
Still, a lot of suffering and oppression has occurred while the long term is unfolding, and not just during Medieval times.
“It was a 100-year struggle during the Industrial Revolution for workers to get any cut of these massive productivity gains in textiles and railways,” Johnson observes. Broader progress has come through increased labor power and electoral government; when the U.S. economy grew spectacularly for three decades after World War II, gains were widely distributed, though that has not been the case recently.

We can get it back, but not with the current form of our machine intelligence obsession. That, we think, is undermining prosperity in the U.S. and around the world.”
A call for “machine usefulness,” not “so-so automation”
What do Acemoglu and Johnson think is deficient about AI? For one thing, they believe the development of AI is too focused on mimicking human intelligence. The scholars are skeptical of the notion that AI mirrors human thinking all told — even things like the chess program AlphaZero, which they regard more as a specialized set of instructions.
Or, for instance, image recognition programs — Is that a husky or a wolf? — use large data sets of past human decisions to build predictive models. But these are often correlation-dependent (a husky is more likely to be in front of your house), and can’t replicate the same cues humans rely on. Researchers know this, of course, and keep refining their tools. But Acemoglu and Robinson contend that many AI programs are less agile than the human mind, and suboptimal replacements for it, even as AI is designed to replace human work.
Acemoglu, who has published many papers on automation and robots, calls these replacement tools “so-so technologies.” A supermarket self-checkout machine does not add meaningful economic productivity; it just transfers work to customers and wealth to shareholders. Another set of AI issues Acemoglu and Johnson are concerned about extend directly into politics: Surveillance technologies, facial-recognition tools, intensive data collection, and AI-spread misinformation.
China deploys AI to create “social credit” scores for citizens, along with heavy surveillance, while tightly restricting freedom of expression. Psychological Benefits: Employment has long been associated with key components of mental health including self-esteem, self-worth, purpose and identity. Automation alone does not determine the future society, because the decisive question is who owns the automated productive systems, data, energy and land, and who therefore receives their output and income. [shard_03094_55120] [shard_02600_20767]  
In the first scenario, automation raises physical productive capacity while access to food, housing, health care and other necessities remains conditional on wages or private wealth. [shard_02600_20767]  
As paid human work disappears, most people lose both purchasing power and their normal route to the goods that machines can abundantly produce, so a society can have full warehouses and widespread deprivation at the same time. [shard_02600_20767]  
Owners of robots, platforms, patents, energy systems and scarce land would capture much of the income, creating a small capital-owning class alongside a permanently unemployed or precariously employed majority. [shard_02600_20767] [shard_03094_55120]  
The market would then become unstable because automated firms can make goods cheaply but cannot profitably sell them to a population without income, encouraging debt, cut-price provision, monopolies and government emergency support rather than a healthy mass-consumer economy. [shard_02600_20767] [shard_03094_55120]  
Population growth would sharpen competition for whatever remains genuinely scarce, especially desirable locations, natural resources, personal attention, political influence and exclusive experiences, even if routine manufactured goods are cheap. [shard_06481_33015]  
Mass joblessness would also be a social crisis rather than merely an income crisis, because employment commonly supplies time structure, relationships, collective activity, status, purpose and identity, and job loss is associated with worsening mental health. [shard_03196_19454]  
A likely political outcome is recurring conflict over ownership and distribution, ranging from labour movements and demands for dividends to riots, populist mobilisation or demands to halt automation. [shard_02600_20767]  
The most dangerous version becomes an automated oligarchy, in which concentrated wealth purchases political influence and surveillance systems are used to manage excluded populations rather than to empower them. [shard_03094_55120]  
Such a regime could be technically efficient yet politically brittle, because economic exclusion and unaccountable automated decisions undermine legitimacy. [shard_02308_27025] [shard_03094_55120]  
A democratic government trying to prevent that outcome would need to separate survival from employment through measures such as a guaranteed income or services, broad ownership of automation, taxes or royalties on automated profits, and strong anti-monopoly rules. [shard_02600_20767] [shard_03094_55120]  
It would also need public auditability of consequential algorithms, appeal rights against automated decisions, data rights, cybersecurity safeguards and human responsibility for systems that allocate benefits, policing, credit or legal outcomes. [shard_02308_27025] [shard_06481_33015]  
Without redistribution, however, this first scenario is not a stable “post-work” society but a society that retains automation while making livelihood dependent on an increasingly unavailable job. [shard_02600_20767]  

In the second scenario, automated production is paired with universal access to the resources required for a dignified life, so food, shelter, health care, education, energy, communications and mobility are guaranteed independently of employment. [shard_00402_65510] [shard_01273_62848]  
This could be organised as universal public services, an unconditional basic income, a social dividend from publicly or broadly owned automated capital, or a combination of these arrangements. [shard_00402_65510] [shard_02600_20767]  
A universal basic income is a periodic unconditional payment made to individuals regardless of wealth or employment, while a universal-resource system can go further by directly guaranteeing essential services. [shard_00402_65510]  
The economic circuit would work because robots supply much of production, the public captures part of the resulting surplus through ownership, taxes, resource rents or dividends, and people receive purchasing power or direct access with which to claim the output.
